title.en: Let an evaluator decide every signal value

summary: Compute node values from the circuit function and render wires from those values, never the other way round.
objective: Make a logic scene correct by construction rather than by matching hand-authored colours.
applies_when: Gates, wires or logic blocks are displayed with signal states.
The viewer can toggle inputs and expects outputs to follow.
A truth table, waveform or readout accompanies the circuit.
example_prompts: Build a gate workbench where flipping an input updates everything downstream.
Show the truth table and the circuit agreeing.
negative_signals: Decorative circuit-like graphics with no logical behaviour.
Sequential circuits with memory, which need a separate clocking discipline.
not_for: Decorative circuit-like graphics with no logical behaviour.
Sequential circuits with memory, which need a separate clocking discipline.

principles: A combinational device produces outputs that depend only on its current inputs, so the entire visible state of a combinational circuit is a function of the input vector. Anything not derived from that function is decoration.

The functional specification can be a truth table or Boolean equations, and both are checkable, which means the scene can verify itself instead of relying on the author having coloured the wires correctly.
Rendering must read from the evaluation. When wire colours are set by hand or by animation, a later edit to the circuit leaves a confidently wrong picture.

Propagation delay is a separate property and a bound rather than a schedule: the longest input-to-output path gives the worst-case time by which outputs have settled, not the time at which every input change reaches them. An animation of a signal travelling is therefore a timing claim that needs its own model.
implementation: Represent the circuit as a graph of typed nodes and evaluate it in dependency order from the current inputs.
Derive wire colour, node highlight and every readout from the evaluated values so they cannot disagree.
Generate the truth table by evaluating the same function over all input combinations rather than typing it in.
If a travelling-signal animation is used, either model a delay per gate or label the animation as illustrative timing.
Detect cycles in a circuit presented as combinational and report them, since a feedback loop is not a combinational function.
observable_checks: Toggle every input in turn and confirm all downstream values update in one consistent step.

Compare the generated truth table against an independently stated specification for the intended function, not only against the circuit that produced it: exhaustive evaluation of the same evaluator proves that the picture and the model agree, which is a weaker result than proving the circuit computes what was intended.
Edit the circuit and confirm the table and colours both change without any manual fix.
Introduce a feedback loop and confirm the scene reports it rather than settling on an arbitrary value.

creative_affordances: Any visual language for signals is fine, including physical metaphors such as water or light, once the evaluator is authoritative.
Deliberately abstract or sculptural circuit layouts remain valid.
known_limits: Authored state-model guidance citing the combinational definition and propagation delay; it does not model electrical behaviour, glitches or fan-out limits.
Sequential behaviour requires the clocking discipline covered separately.

claims.statement: A combinational device has outputs that depend only on its current inputs, its functional specification can be given as a truth table or Boolean equations, and its propagation delay corresponds to the longest path from inputs to outputs.
claims.scope: Digital combinational logic; it does not describe sequential circuits, analogue behaviour or physical timing margins.

source_refs.locator: 4.1, combinational device definition, functional specification and propagation delay
